This invisible gas controls ₹40+ lakh crore of global industries.

And almost no one in India is paying attention.

That should worry you.

Everyone debates oil.
Everyone tracks semiconductors.

But helium?

Ignored.

And that’s exactly the problem.

Here’s the uncomfortable truth:

India imports nearly 100% of its helium.

No reserves.
No serious conversation.
No urgency.

Meanwhile,

• Qatar controls ~30% of the global supply
• Geopolitical tensions are rising
• Prices are already up 20–40%

And this gas powers:

– MRI machines
– Semiconductor fabs
– Critical research

So let’s ask the real question:

👉 Why are we pushing semiconductor ambitions…
without securing critical inputs like helium?

This isn’t just a supply issue.

It’s a strategy gap.

We’ve seen this before:

APIs.
Semiconductors.
Energy.

We react after the crisis.

The difference this time?

Helium isn’t replaceable.

Once it’s gone, it’s gone.

Most people will ignore this.

A few will connect the dots early.

Which side are you on?

And the crazy part?

Their resume was actually good.

Most job seekers rely on only one strategy:

Apply → Wait → Hope.

But many interviews actually happen because someone:

Global risk is real - oil is the switch
Stop scrolling - 3 charts every investor and policy-maker should see

I just completed a 30-page briefing with 20+ charts on the interconnected geopolitical crisis: USA-Iran tensions, Venezuela, Russia-China coordination, and Taiwan risk. These events are not isolated - they interact and feed into oil, currency, and market shocks that could reshape emerging markets, especially India.

Key takeaways:
• Immediate shock variable: disruption through the Strait of Hormuz could push Brent above $100 within days (see oil scenarios, pages 16-17).
• Venezuela - China - Iran: regime change in Venezuela rewires crude flows and sanctions-evasion channels (flow diagram, page 8).
• Tech and information warfare: targeted IPv6 blackout signals a new model of selective internet shutdowns (technical note, page 23).
• India impact: oil is the main driver of the rupee, inflation and FPI flows - base case sees oil easing to ~USD 50 by mid-2026; risk case is materially worse (India scenarios, pages 17-19).

Why this matters:
This is a web of risks, not separate problems. Investors should position for commodity and FX volatility and stress-test portfolios. Policy-makers should fast-track contingency planning for energy and remittances. Market strategists should focus on scenario planning rather than short-term forecasting.

Read the full briefing (30 pages, 20+ charts) - PDF attached to this post.
